title: Decide whether to add an external dead-man's-switch for the cron loops
description:
WHY (needs Kevin, not an agent): the cron health auditor built on 2026-09-06 runs on the same machine, from the same binary family, and reports through the same AgenC server as the crons it watches. A failure that takes out AgenC takes out its watchdog. That shared-fate gap is real and cannot be closed from inside AgenC.

The ops-world answer is an external dead-man's-switch: an outside service alerts on the ABSENCE of a success ping inside an expected window. A parallel research mission found no agent-ecosystem prior art for this — Anthropic's own cloud Routines silently failed for 28 days while reporting success (github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/54260, closed as not planned) — but ops-land solved it long ago. Healthchecks.io was named, free tier covering seven crons.

THE ORDERING IS THE WHOLE MECHANISM: the ping must fire only AFTER the job verifies its own deliverable exists. A naive 'the process ran' ping would have reported success on all nine of the ten hn-daily-pull runs that silently delivered nothing — those processes exited fine, they just produced no output.

'agenc cron doctor' is already shaped to be that ping's source: it exits 0 only when every cron has actually delivered, non-zero otherwise. Wiring it up is a one-line change to the scheduled command.

CONSTRAINT: this means signing up for a third-party service and sending it a heartbeat, which is Kevin's call. Deliberately not provisioned by the mission that found the gap.

ACCEPTANCE: Kevin has decided yes or no. If yes, an external monitor alerts him when the doctor stops reporting all-clear, verified by withholding a ping and confirming the alert arrives on a channel he actually reads.
notes:
CITATION CORRECTION (2026-09-06, relayed from coordinator 5da13a09 after independent verification against primaries): the description's characterisation of github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/54260 is wrong in its framing. The factual core holds — the issue is real, the 28-day silent failure is real, run_once_fired is the mechanism, and the state is NOT_PLANNED — but the REPORTER closed it himself as a duplicate, eight minutes after a bot flagged it. It was not Anthropic waving it away, and it should not be cited as a vendor ignoring silent failure.

Prefer issue 48725 as the citation for that point: it is the canonical one, it was labelled 'regression' by Anthropic engineering, and it was then closed not-planned as stale. Better evidence and an honest one.

Separate calibration note on the source report (~/app/exobrain/project-support/2026-09-06_background-agent-systems-research/README.md): its per-claim source tags are rigorous and twelve of twelve citations held against primaries, but its per-RECOMMENDATION confidence drifts upward — two recommendations are marked High while every source beneath them is tagged [claimed] rather than [demonstrated]. Read the recommendation-level confidence as softer than it reads. The null result on YC's QM was independently reproduced.

title: Root cause of the launchd LWCR failure that bricked six crons is still unidentified
description:
WHY: on 2026-09-06 six of seven crons were found failing at launchd spawn time, every scheduled slot since 2026-09-01, silently. The mechanism is proven — xpcproxy could not resolve the job's Lightweight Code Requirement ('Unable to update LWCR with smd: 3'), so launchd aborted the spawn before agenc ran, reporting EX_CONFIG 78 or OS_REASON_CODESIGNING. Reloading the job (bootout + bootstrap) fixes it. What TRIGGERS the LWCR going stale is NOT known.

The strongest correlate is that /Users/odyssey/app/agenc/_build/agenc was rebuilt at 2026-09-01 13:55, and the single surviving cron was the only one whose launchd job had been bootstrapped after that moment (its 'runs' counter, which resets on bootstrap, showed exactly the days since). But the obvious hypothesis was TESTED AND REFUTED: two launchd jobs were bootstrapped against a small ad-hoc-signed Go binary, the binary was rebuilt so its CDHash changed, and both jobs still ran fine. So replacing the binary is not by itself sufficient. The machine had been up since 2026-08-21, so a reboot is not the trigger either.

This matters because the current fix is detect-and-repair, which is the right design given an unknown trigger but leaves a window: between the trigger firing and the auditor's next 15-minute pass, a cron whose slot falls in that window loses its run.

ACCEPTANCE: either the trigger is identified and eliminated at the source, or it is established that detect-and-repair is the appropriate permanent answer and that conclusion is written down with its evidence. Watch for recurrence — the auditor now logs to ~/.agenc/logs/cron-doctor.log, so a second occurrence will be dated and correlatable against what else happened on the machine.

Background: docs/incidents/2026-09-06-silent-cron-outage.md in the AgenC repo.

title: Review Yannik's PR #40 (APFS clones for mission repo copies) before merging
description:
GOAL: PR #40 (https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/pull/40, by ro0mquy / Yannik) claims mission creation drops from 5.8s to 0.1s by copying mission repos with APFS clones. Kevin wants confidence the speedup is safe before it lands, and he does not extend that confidence to the PR's authoring agent. His words, near-verbatim (Todoist capture 2026-09-05): "I'm cautious of what he's doing - it sounds like it's tricky hardlinking stuff. Also, his Claude is almost definitely not as rigorous as my Claude; I'd want my Claude to explore the branch/PR." The interest is a grounded merge / don't-merge verdict, not a checklist pass.

CONSTRAINTS: Read the actual branch, not just the PR description or the diff summary — the concern is about runtime behavior a diff will not state. Any GitHub post (review, comment) goes through /github-posting, which owns the mandatory AgenC-authored disclosure prefix. Merging is Kevin's call, not the reviewer's.

CONTEXT: Mission repo clones are load-bearing for every AgenC mission — the isolation guarantee AgenC advertises depends on each mission getting its own working copy. Kevin's caution is about that guarantee, so failure modes that break isolation weigh more than performance regressions.

PROVENANCE: routed from Todoist inbox during AgenC mission 2e94e194-6341-44a5-8c51-062bebb845df. Tracked in Todoist as the project "Merge Yannik's APFS mission-clone PR" under Not This Week.
acceptance_criteria: A written merge / don't-merge verdict Kevin can act on, that names the concrete failure modes an APFS-clone or hardlink-based repo copy could introduce for AgenC missions — what a clone sees when the source repo changes underneath it, what git observes inside the clone, behavior on non-APFS or cross-filesystem targets, and cleanup/teardown semantics — and states for each whether the PR handles it. Every claim cites branch code by file and line, not the PR description.

title: Make work assignable to missions, and force parents to assign it
description:
When a parent mission spawns a child today, what the child is supposed to accomplish exists only as prose in the spawn prompt. Nothing links the mission to a tracked work item, which costs three things at once: you cannot ask 'what is mission X working on' without reading its transcript, you cannot ask 'what mission is bead Y being worked in', and the parent's accountability for the child's outcome is a matter of how carefully the prompt was written rather than something the system knows about.

Kevin wants work items — beads and Todoist tasks — to be first-class assignable to missions, and then a hook that requires a parent mission to make that assignment when it spawns a child, rather than leaving it to whether the parent thought of it. The hook is the enforcement half of the same intent, not a separate idea: the assignment only becomes reliable infrastructure once it stops depending on an agent remembering. That is the same reasoning as CLAUDE.md's preference for deterministic enforcement over guidance an agent has to recall.

Live example from the session that produced this bead: two dotfiles missions were spawned to own dotfiles-eqv6 and dotfiles-p9xr. Both briefs name their bead in prose and both missions report back by message. It works, and it is exactly the informal pattern this bead replaces — nothing but the prose connects mission 32dc359a to its bead, and nothing would have caught it if the brief had forgotten to say.

Worth weighing while designing: what happens to spawns that legitimately have no trackable work yet (blank missions, exploration, a mission whose first job is to figure out what the work even is) — a hook that cannot express that case will get worked around, which is worse than no hook.

Captured by Kevin in his Todoist inbox 2026-09-04, routed here during inbox processing (AgenC mission 468961df-c2be-4e79-baf3-6026563c6dc7). Related: agenc-koge, which wants mission work queryable without reading transcripts — assignment is one of the things that would make that query answerable, so these two should be designed with each other in view.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance criteria: (1) A bead or Todoist task can be assigned to a mission, and the link is queryable from both directions — given a mission, what work it owns; given a work item, what mission owns it. (2) A hook prevents a parent mission from spawning a child without assigned work, and its denial text tells the agent how to comply rather than merely refusing. (3) Spawns with genuinely no assignable work are expressible without disabling the hook — demonstrate the escape hatch and why it cannot be used as a routine bypass. (4) Demonstrated end-to-end with a real parent/child mission pair, not unit-tested in isolation.

title: Give each mission a queryable summary of what it worked on
description:
Today the only way to find out what a past mission did is to replay its transcript. That is expensive for a human and often flatly impossible for an agent working inside a context budget — so in practice prior missions are invisible, and agents redo work, re-derive conclusions, or miss that the thing they are about to build already exists.

The interest is making the mission database answerable: an agent should be able to ask 'what has been going on lately' or 'has anything touched X' and get useful answers cheaply, without reading transcripts. Kevin's framing was auto-summarization — each mission carrying a summary of what it was working on — but the underlying need is queryability, and if the better shape is structured metadata, extracted topics, embeddings, or something else entirely, take it there.

Worth weighing while designing: when the summary gets written (mission end is the obvious moment, but missions also die, hang, or run for days), and what makes a summary actually useful to a future agent versus merely present.

Captured by Kevin in his Todoist inbox 2026-09-01, routed here during inbox processing (AgenC mission 468961df-c2be-4e79-baf3-6026563c6dc7). Related: agenc-eawz, the other mission-coordination bead from the same capture batch.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance criteria: (1) A mission's record carries a summary of what it worked on, produced without a human writing it. (2) An agent in a fresh mission can query the mission database and get that summary back without reading any transcript. (3) The summary is good enough that a fresh agent reading it can correctly decide whether it needs to go read the full transcript — tested against at least a few real past missions, not synthetic ones. (4) Summaries exist for missions that ended abnormally, or the gap is explicitly documented as out of scope.

title: Let missions react to another mission going idle
description:
A mission that depends on work happening in another mission currently has no way to learn that the other mission has finished. The only routes are polling on a timer or a human relaying the news, and both burn attention that the system exists to save — the dependent agent either wastes tokens checking, or stalls until Kevin notices and pokes it. The interest here is autonomous chaining: a mission should be able to express that it cares about another mission reaching idle, and be woken when that happens, so multi-mission work composes without a human in the loop.

Idle is the chosen signal because it is the observable that already means 'this agent has stopped working and is waiting' — but if a better-defined completion signal exists or should exist in the mission lifecycle, that is a legitimate place to take this.

Captured by Kevin in his Todoist inbox 2026-09-01, routed here during inbox processing (AgenC mission 468961df-c2be-4e79-baf3-6026563c6dc7).
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance criteria: (1) A running mission can register interest in another mission's transition to idle, addressing that mission by an identifier it can actually obtain at runtime. (2) When the watched mission goes idle, the watching mission is woken and can act, without having polled. (3) Demonstrated end-to-end with two real missions, not just unit-tested. (4) Existing mission messaging and lifecycle behavior are unchanged for missions that do not use the feature.

title: A headless mission stalls forever, silently, when it hits a permission prompt
description:
## Why
A mission spawned with --headless has nobody who can answer a permission prompt. When it reaches a gated operation it enters WAITING and stays there indefinitely. Nothing errors, nothing times out, and no notification is raised — from the outside it is indistinguishable from a mission doing slow work.

This defeats the purpose of headless. Headless exists so work can run without occupying an attached slot or a human's screen, but any headless mission that touches a gated operation is a mission that will silently stop, usually at the end, after all the expensive work is done.

## Observed
Mission c3dfb42d, spawned --headless, completed a large body of work (two repos, multiple review rounds, all CI green), then announced 'Merging. Fork first.', issued the merge, and entered WAITING. It sat there ~80 minutes. A SendMessage nudge did not wake it. A synchronous  cleared the state, after which it resumed, reached the same merge, and stalled again within about five minutes — confirming the cause is the gated operation rather than a transient hang.

Resolved only by a different, attached session performing the merges on its behalf.

Note the interaction with : it reports 'Reload queued (will fire on Claude's next idle)', which is inert for a stalled mission, since a mission blocked on a prompt may never reach idle. The async form assumes the liveness that a stall violates.

## Why it is worse than an ordinary block
The failure is silent and it is end-loaded. It surfaces after the work is done rather than before it starts, so the cost is already sunk when it hits. And a parent coordinating the mission cannot distinguish it from progress without knowing to poll for a WAITING state specifically — see agenc-5jxx, where a watcher polling BUSY/IDLE/STOPPED never fired because WAITING matched none of them.

## Directions worth weighing (not prescriptions)
Whether a headless mission should fail fast on a gated operation rather than blocking, so the cost surfaces immediately. Whether it should raise a notification that a human or parent can act on, turning a silent stall into a request. Whether spawning headless should surface which operations will be ungated, so the caller knows before committing the work. Whether an attached parent should be able to answer a child's prompt.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A headless mission that reaches a gated operation produces a signal a human or a parent mission can observe, rather than stalling silently
- The state is distinguishable from ordinary slow work without the observer having to know the harness's full status vocabulary in advance
- The documented recovery path works on a mission that is actually stalled

## Provenance
AgenC mission 591187e7-dab6-4b2d-a063-ff12220d4c3a, 2026-09-01, coordinating c3dfb42d-e632-4bd3-9a49-8bb4fca97e50. Related: agenc-5jxx (block-on-mission-state; same incident, the detection half), agenc-e7cs (mission detach bug, same session).

title: Stop emitting ANSI colour codes in command output
description:
## Why
AgenC's command output is now overwhelmingly consumed by agents rather than read by humans. Kevin's framing: it is basically no longer run by humans, it is run and consumed by agents. Colour codes are ergonomics for a reader who is mostly no longer there, and they actively break the consumer who is.

They break it in the worst way — silently. An agent parsing `agenc mission ls` gets `\033[94mIDLE\033[0m` in the status field, not `IDLE`, so a string comparison against `IDLE` or `STOPPED` is simply always false. Nothing errors. The parse just quietly never matches.

## The incident this comes from
A parent mission coordinating a child armed three background watchers, each containing a branch of the form `if [ "$ST" = "STOPPED" ]`. That branch never fired in any of them. Two of the three appeared to work because their success path was triggered by a GitHub API call while only the stall path depended on parsing — so the broken half was masked. The failure was invisible and pointed the safe-looking way: a dead child and a healthy child produced identical output, namely silence. Kevin noticed the parent had gone quiet before the parent did.

Full write-up and the wider coordination problem: bead agenc-5jxx.

## What is wanted
Kevin's decision is to remove the colour codes rather than make them conditional. The reasoning is that the human-reader case barely exists any more, so carrying conditional-colour machinery would be complexity serving almost nobody.

Raise it with him before implementing if you find that wrong — the conventional alternative is to emit colour only when stdout is a terminal, which costs nothing here because `github.com/mattn/go-isatty` is already a dependency and already used for stdin checks in `cmd/first_run.go` and `cmd/notifications_create.go`. That would keep interactive colour and still fix every piped consumer, since a captured pipe is not a TTY. Kevin has heard the removal framing and chosen it; do not silently substitute the alternative, but do surface it if the codebase gives you a reason he has not seen.

## What the codebase looks like
`cmd/ansi_colors.go` centralises the constants, which is a natural seam. But nine files contain raw escapes and at least one — `cmd/tmux_palette.go:333` — hardcodes the sequence inline instead of using a constant, so a constants-only change would miss it. Note that the tmux palette is a genuinely interactive surface and may be the one place colour still earns its keep; decide that deliberately rather than by whether it happened to use the constant.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Piped output from AgenC commands contains no ANSI escape sequences — verify by capturing to a file and inspecting bytes (`od -c`), not by eye, since a terminal renders escapes invisibly
- The check covers commands agents actually parse, at minimum `mission ls`, `mission peers`, `repo ls`, `mission inspect`
- Inline escapes are covered, not just uses of the shared constants
- Whatever is decided for genuinely interactive surfaces is stated and deliberate, not incidental

## Provenance
Requested by Kevin 2026-09-01. Field evidence from AgenC mission 591187e7-dab6-4b2d-a063-ff12220d4c3a coordinating child mission c3dfb42d. Related: agenc-5jxx (block-on-mission-state, same root incident), agenc-e7cs (mission detach bug, same session).
notes:
2026-09-01 SCOPE CLARIFICATION from Kevin, mid-execution: it is the agenc CLI output — what running 'agenc <something>' produces — that is consumed purely by agents. He STILL USES THE COMMAND PALETTE HEAVILY, so that is a genuinely interactive human surface and KEEPS ITS COLOUR. Do not strip cmd/tmux_palette.go.

This sharpens rather than contradicts the original framing: the dividing line is not which file happens to use the shared constant, it is whether a human or an agent reads the output. Piped command output: no escapes. Palette and other interactive TUI surfaces: unchanged.

Consequence to check rather than assume: the split may not be clean along file boundaries. Any code path shared between a palette rendering and a plain command's output needs to know which context it is in rather than being stripped globally. If the split turns out messy, propose where to draw the line rather than guessing — Kevin follows this closely and would rather be asked.

Added acceptance criterion (mirror of the existing one): confirm the palette STILL emits colour after the change, verified rather than assumed, so both halves can be shown — not just the half that was set out to be fixed. The CLI half's criterion is unchanged: capture to a file and inspect bytes with od -c, never visual inspection, since escapes render invisibly and that is how the original bug hid.

Relayed to mission 2c644c10 while it was mid-work.
2026-09-01: Kevin reviewed PR #37 and approved it; instructed that the mission merge it. He will rebuild the agenc binary himself afterwards (compiled Go — the fix does not take effect in his installed binary until then).

VERIFIED BY 591187e7 BEFORE APPROVAL RELAY, not relayed on trust: PR #37 open at head dfe0aca, 13 files, +213/-32. Both directions genuinely asserted in Go unit tests — TestColorizeStatus_KeepsAnsiForPicker and TestFormatRepoDisplayForPicker_KeepsAnsi assert colour PRESENT; the stdout-side tests assert no escapes in command output. cmd/tmux_palette.go is untouched, so the deliberately-kept inline escape survives. Note PR #37 carries no CI checks, but that is this repo's normal state rather than a gap introduced here — agenc has only release.yml and no PR CI workflow, and recently merged PRs #34 and #35 likewise show no checks; the guarantees live in Go unit tests run under 'make check' and the pre-commit hook.

DESIGN NOTE WORTH KEEPING: the mission solved the shared-formatter problem better than the brief specified. Three formatters (repo display, repo-name, status colouriser) were each shared between a stdout table and an fzf picker. Rather than making them conditional at runtime, it made the PLAIN form the default and added destination-named colouring variants (formatRepoDisplayForPicker, displayGitRepoForPicker), so a stdout caller cannot pick up colour by accident. It then re-checked every remaining call site by reading where output actually goes rather than by assumption, which caught one picker misfiled as stdout in repo_helpers.go.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #37 (https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/pull/37), branch mieubrisse/agenc-hxr4-no-ansi-in-command-output. Command output carries no ANSI escapes; interactive fzf/palette surfaces keep colour per Kevin's confirmation. Verified byte-level via new E2E section, Go unit tests on both halves, and manual od -c against the real instance. Follow-up agenc-afp8 for documenting the convention.

title: Let a mission block on another mission reaching a terminal state
description:
## Why
A mission that spawns or coordinates another mission has no supported way to wait for it. Today the parent must hand-roll a poller against `agenc mission ls`, and that output is formatted for humans — which makes the poller quietly wrong in a way that is invisible at runtime.

Kevin has a Todoist task tracking this idea (added 2026-09-01); this bead carries the field evidence for why it matters.

## The incident this bead exists for
While coordinating a child mission (YNAB server work, mission c3dfb42d) from a parent (mission 591187e7), the parent armed three separate background watchers to learn when the child finished or died. Each contained a stall-detection branch of roughly this shape:

    ST=$(agenc mission ls | grep -E '^c3dfb42d' | awk '{print $4}')
    if [ "$ST" = "STOPPED" ]; then ...

That branch never fired in any of the three, because `agenc mission ls` emits ANSI colour codes. Field 4 is not `IDLE` but `\033[94mIDLE\033[0m`, so the comparison is always false. Confirmed with `od -c`.

Two properties made this worse than an ordinary bug. First, it failed silently and in the safe-looking direction: a dead child and a working child produce identical output — nothing. Second, two of the three watchers appeared to work, because their success path was triggered by a GitHub API call while only the stall path depended on parsing. So the broken half was masked by the working half. Kevin noticed the parent had gone quiet before the parent did, which is the opposite of the intended arrangement.

The parent had also told Kevin, in writing, that a stall would report itself. It would not have.

## What is actually needed
A first-class way for one mission to wait on another reaching a terminal state, so that coordination does not depend on every agent independently reinventing a poller over human-formatted output. The distinction that matters to a caller is *completed* versus *died or stalled* — a primitive that cannot tell those apart pushes the problem back to the caller.

Worth considering as a cheaper partial fix even if the blocking primitive is not built: machine-readable output (a `--json` flag on `mission ls`, or colour suppression when stdout is not a TTY) removes this entire class of parsing bug without any new concept. Note that colour was already being emitted into a captured, non-TTY pipe, which is itself the smell.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A mission can wait for another mission to reach a terminal state without polling human-formatted CLI output
- Completion and death/stall are distinguishable outcomes to the waiter, not a single "it stopped" signal
- A waiter cannot be silently disabled by output formatting — either the output is machine-readable, or the wait is not built on parsing it at all
- Waiting does not require the parent to hold a busy loop that consumes its own context

## Provenance
Field evidence from AgenC mission 591187e7-dab6-4b2d-a063-ff12220d4c3a (2026-09-01), coordinating child mission c3dfb42d-e632-4bd3-9a49-8bb4fca97e50. Related existing bug, found in the same session: agenc-e7cs (`mission detach` fails when the pane's window was already unlinked from the recorded session).
notes:
2026-09-01 SECOND FIELD INCIDENT, and a sharper one than the original. Mission c3dfb42d went silent in WAITING status for ~80 minutes with its work already COMPLETE — both PRs green, reviews addressed, nothing blocking. Its last recorded action was a polling loop waiting on PR checks that had already passed (23s and 38s runs, long finished). The parent (591187e7) did not notice; Kevin's standing expectation is that the parent drives these missions, and instead the parent's watcher reported a clean timeout while the child sat stuck.

WATCHER FLAW, third distinct one this session and the worst: the watcher polled for BUSY, IDLE and STOPPED. WAITING matched none of them, so the stall condition was unreachable and the loop ran its full 70-minute window before reporting TIMEOUT rather than STALL. Note the pattern across all three of this session's watcher bugs — the success path was always correct and the FAILURE path was always broken, which is precisely the asymmetry that makes a broken watcher indistinguishable from a working one. Design implication for this bead: a wait primitive must enumerate every terminal and stuck state the harness can produce, and a caller should not have to know the full state vocabulary to write a correct wait. If AgenC exposes waiting, the states it can return are part of the contract.

Fixed watcher validated: treats WAITING for 5 consecutive minutes as a stall and detected it in ~5 minutes instead of 70.

RECOVERY DATA for the primitive's design: a SendMessage nudge did NOT wake the stalled mission. 'agenc mission reload --async' reported 'Reload queued (will fire on Claude's next idle)' — which is useless for exactly this case, since a stuck mission may never reach idle; the async queueing assumes liveness that a stall violates. A SYNCHRONOUS 'agenc mission reload' cleared it immediately. Worth building into whatever wait primitive lands: detecting the stall is only half of it, and the documented recovery path (async reload) is the one that does not work on a stalled mission.
2026-09-01 THIRD FIELD INCIDENT, and a NEW failure shape distinct from the previous two. Mission f72f85f5 sat at status BUSY for one hour with zero activity — last transcript entry 18:19, checked at 19:19. It had received a message at 18:19 and never acted on it: no reload performed, no PR opened, no further tool calls. Recovered by a synchronous 'agenc mission reload' from the parent.

THE LESSON, which sharpens this bead's requirements: STATUS IS NOT LIVENESS. The three stalls in this workstream presented as three different statuses — STOPPED (dead), WAITING (blocked on a permission prompt nobody could answer, agenc-7ech), and now BUSY (hung while nominally working). A waiter that keys on status alone cannot detect the third, and BUSY is the most dangerous of the three because it is indistinguishable from healthy work and is what a naive implementation would treat as 'still going, keep waiting'.

WATCHER CORRECTION: the parent's watcher now also tracks the ACTIVITY CLOCK — the timestamp of the last transcript entry — and reports a stall when it goes stale (~12m) REGARDLESS of reported status. That is the check that would have caught this an hour earlier. Design implication for any wait primitive AgenC exposes: liveness must be derived from observed progress, not from a state label, and the primitive should surface 'no progress for N' as a first-class outcome alongside completion and death.

RUNNING TALLY of failure shapes this bead must cover, all observed in one workstream in two days: died; blocked on an unanswerable prompt (headless); hung while BUSY; plus the original detection failure where the parent's own parser could not represent WAITING at all. Recovery data: SendMessage nudge does not clear a stall; 'reload --async' is inert (queues for an idle that never comes); synchronous 'reload' cleared all of them.

title: Let a running mission be moved between tmux sessions
description:
Today, attaching a mission to a different tmux session means manually attaching it there and then detaching it from the one it is currently in — a fiddly two-step done by hand. Nothing is at risk (missions live in the background AgenC pool and are never killed by this), so the cost is pure friction, not fragility.

The interest behind the request is larger than the convenience: Kevin wants Claude to be able to manipulate his WORKSPACE STATE — specifically, which missions are attached to which tmux session — so that reorganizing how he is working becomes something he can delegate in a sentence rather than perform by hand. A single agent-drivable move operation is the necessary first step toward that. Design for that end state, not just for the manual hassle.

Captured from Todoist inbox 2026-08-31, routed 2026-09-01.
acceptance_criteria: Acceptance criteria: (1) an attached mission can be moved from one tmux session to another as a single operation, without a separate attach-then-detach dance; (2) the operation is drivable by an agent, not interactive-only, so Claude can invoke it; (3) the mission keeps running and keeps its Claude session and state across the move; (4) exercised end-to-end on a live mission.

title: Cron missions that die before completing produce no signal — the loop silently stops delivering
description:
A cron-fired mission that dies mid-run (API connection error, model-unavailable error, hung tool) leaves no trace anywhere Kevin looks. The mission shows STOPPED in 'agenc mission ls' — indistinguishable from a healthy completed run — and no notification is posted, so the only way to learn that a scheduled loop stopped delivering is to notice the absence of an artifact that was never loud in the first place.

Observed concretely on hn-daily-pull: 3 of the last 6 runs died before posting anything. 2026-08-26 (90e21a58) died on 'API Error: Unable to connect to API (ENOTFOUND)'. 2026-08-30 (3052f4f1) died on 'claude-sonnet-5[1m] is temporarily unavailable, so auto mode cannot determine the safety of Skill'. Both look identical to a successful run in the mission list. The 2026-08-29 run noted the same pattern in claude-news-processor and called it beads-worthy against AgenC.

This is the silent-rot failure mode Kevin's CLAUDE.md names directly (Pair Every Loop With a Check-Loop, and Patch Register P-4 Fail loudly, not silently): a working system emits no signal that it has stopped doing its job, so absence of an error reads as correctness. The cost compounds — the digest window is capped at 48h, so a dead run permanently loses coverage of the stories in its window. The 2026-08-29 02:00 to 2026-08-30 02:07 slice was never covered by any digest and cannot be recovered.

WHY this matters more than the individual crons: every AgenC cron loop Kevin builds inherits this. Fixing it once at the platform level is what makes fire-and-forget scheduled work trustworthy enough to keep building on.
design: Deliberately not prescribing the mechanism. The obvious shapes (AgenC posts a failure notification when a cron mission terminates without its expected completion signal; a health-check cron that audits recent cron history for anomalous exits; distinguishing 'completed' from 'died' in mission status) each have tradeoffs the implementer should weigh — notably how AgenC knows a mission ENDED BADLY versus merely ended, given a cron skill's success criteria live in the skill, not the platform. Whoever picks this up should design the signal, not just bolt on a retry.
acceptance_criteria: A cron-fired mission that dies before completing its work surfaces that fact through a channel Kevin actually watches, without him having to go look. Verified by inducing a mid-run failure in a real cron mission and confirming the signal arrives. Distinguishing a dead run from a healthy one must not require reading the transcript.
notes:
Surfaced by the hn-daily-pull cron run 2026-09-01, mission 787a113c-6c58-4657-9f46-38b6ebbb16a9, during its longitudinal read of the prior 5 runs.

Related but distinct signal found in the same read: every hn-digest notification from 2026-07-14 onward (18 consecutive) is unread, while Kevin marks 88 of 139 notifications read across all kinds. That is a delivery/attention question about the notification channel itself, not about silent death — tracked here only as context.

ADDRESSED 2026-09-06 by mission 10a97e0b-7234-4a6c-b938-d1ce40c64fb8, branch mieubrisse/agenc-cron-doctor (commit 32cc218). NOT YET MERGED — leaving open until Kevin reviews.

The mechanism: 'agenc cron doctor' audits every enabled cron and posts a cron.health notification. Three checks at the spawn layer — launchd has no job registered; launchd's last spawn failed; the last scheduled fire produced no mission. Plus the one this bead asked for: did the most recent finished run do any work.

The discriminator was the hard part. A PostToolUse event in the mission's wrapper.log. The mission row is useless for this (status is computed at read time; prompt_count is 1 for dead and healthy runs alike). The Stop hook looks like the obvious answer and is WRONG — measured across recent missions, several that made 30-82 tool calls logged zero Stop events, so keying on Stop reports healthy crons as dead. idle_prompt fires even for runs that died at spawn. Zero tool calls is also semantically right: a skill that read nothing, called nothing and wrote nothing delivered nothing.

Verified by induction, not reasoning: spawned a real daily-state-summary run and killed it before it made a tool call (wrapper.log came out 546 bytes, 0 PostToolUse — the exact shape of 3052f4f1, the run exobrain-6g1 recorded as dying on model-unavailable). The scheduled auditor reported it and posted the notification. Separately, on its first live run the auditor caught two genuinely dead runs nobody had asked it to look for.

Now running as launchd job 'agenc-doctor' every 15 min against a bridge binary at ~/.agenc/bin/agenc-doctor built from the branch.

title: Missions spawned in a test environment hit Claude Code first-run onboarding instead of the existing login
description:
Observed 2026-08-30 in mission f2f47c6a-638b-4892-988c-a82041d27da9 while verifying agenc-padz.

WHAT HAPPENED: 'agenc-test mission new --blank --prompt ...' created mission 8f8f7b81 and launched Claude in the pool window, but instead of starting a session, Claude presented its first-run flow — the theme picker, then the 'Select login method' screen. The wrapper stayed RUNNING, no Claude session ever registered, and the mission was unusable.

THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT MAKES THIS LOOK LIKE AN AGENC DEFECT RATHER THAN A CLAUDE CODE ONE: a plain 'claude' started by hand in that same mission's agent/ directory, in a tmux window in the same pool session, came up normally — 'Welcome back Kevin!', authenticated, no onboarding. Same binary (/opt/homebrew/bin/claude), same HOME, no CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR in either. The only difference visible in the process line was AgenC's '--settings <mission>/agenc-settings.json'.

WHY IT MATTERS: it makes 'make e2e'-adjacent manual testing of anything that needs a live Claude in the test environment impossible without hand-driving the onboarding, and hand-driving it risks touching the real ~/.claude login state. It may also affect real missions under conditions not yet identified — 'theme' is null in ~/.claude.json, which is what appears to trigger the theme picker, and that null is not test-environment-specific.

WORTH CHECKING FIRST: whether the generated op-settings file (or the sandbox block inside it) is what diverts Claude off its existing credentials, and whether the trust-seeding step behaves differently for a test-environment mission directory.
acceptance_criteria: A mission created in the test environment starts a usable Claude session without presenting first-run onboarding, verified by 'agenc-test mission new' followed by the mission appearing in 'agenc mission peers'. If the cause turns out to be environmental rather than an AgenC defect, the finding is recorded and the bead closed with that explanation rather than silently dropped.

title: Expose mission UUID -> Claude Code peer name so agents can address each other via SendMessage
description:
Agents inside missions increasingly need to message each other, and Claude Code's built-in SendMessage is the right channel for it. But SendMessage addresses peers by a per-session derived name (e.g. 'agent-da') that carries no mission, repo, or task identity, while an agent knows its counterpart only by AgenC mission UUID. Nothing in AgenC bridges the two: 'agenc session ls' stops at the session UUID and never surfaces the peer name, and 'agenc tmux resolve-mission' only works pane-by-pane.

WHY THIS MATTERS: without a bridge, agents either fall back to 'agenc mission send-keys' (types into a tmux pane, bypassing the messaging protocol entirely) or reach into Claude Code's private session registry at ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json, which is an undocumented internal that can change shape on any Claude Code release. The skill /agenc-mission-messaging currently ships the registry-reading workaround and documents it as depending on Claude Code 2.1.224 / peerProtocol 1. That is a known-fragile dependency sitting in the middle of what is becoming a frequent operation.

The desired end state is that an agent holding a mission UUID can obtain the exact string SendMessage needs, from a supported AgenC surface, without touching Claude Code internals. How to get there is open - it may be a new subcommand, additional columns on an existing one, or something better. Note the peer address is currently name-plus-ref ('agent-da [bd93b3]'), and cross-session peers reject the bare name on first contact, so whatever AgenC exposes should account for the ref rather than just the name.
design:
Design findings from mission 7dd882f8 (2026-08-30), verified against the agenc source at cmd/mission_ls.go, cmd/mission_inspect.go, internal/claudeconfig/, and the live registry.

WHERE IT FITS: internal/claudeconfig/ is already the package that sequesters knowledge of Claude Code's on-disk layout (build.go encodes the ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-agent-dir> transcript path scheme). The registry-reading logic belongs there for the same reason, so exactly one file in agenc knows the format and both commands call it. Kevin's stated architectural goal is to sequester all Claude Code reading and oddities inside agenc rather than letting skills and agents learn them.

SURFACING: cmd/mission_ls.go already builds a variant table with a PANE column (ID, LAST PROMPT, STATUS, PANE, SESSION, REPO), so a PEER column is a precedented move rather than a new concept. mission ls answers 'who can I talk to right now'; mission inspect answers 'what is this specific mission's address'. Both are wanted; ls is the higher-value one because it makes peers discoverable without knowing a UUID first.

COST IS NOT A CONCERN: the registry holds one small JSON file per LIVE session (8 at time of writing), not per mission (2,830 mission directories exist). The work is one directory read plus a handful of small file reads, and it does not scale with mission count. mission ls already queries the agenc server for status, which is more expensive than this.

THE WRINKLE THAT LIMITS SCOPE: the working SendMessage address is two parts, a name (agent-da) plus a short hex ref (bd93b3). Only the name is present in the registry file. The ref could not be derived from the record's fields, and three bounded attempts at locating its derivation in the Claude Code binary did not settle it. What IS established: refs are stable across observers - two different sessions independently saw the same peer as 'agent-de [402f16]' - so a ref is a property of the peer, not of who is asking. Consequence: an agenc command can supply the name today, which removes file-format knowledge from every skill and agent, but an agent would still need one ListAgents call (or one rejected send) to obtain the ref. That is partial sequestration, and worth shipping anyway; whether full sequestration is reachable depends on settling the ref derivation, which would itself be reverse-engineered and therefore fragile in the same way the current workaround is.
acceptance_criteria:
An agent that needs to message another mission can do so using AgenC tooling plus the ListAgents tool, without reading anything under ~/.claude/ itself. Requiring a ListAgents call is explicitly acceptable — Kevin scoped it that way on 2026-08-30: 'our work is just to make sure that AgenC has the tooling needed in order to allow agents to send messages to other agents, even if it does require a call to the ListAgents tool. We really just need a way for agents to make sense of the ListAgents output.'

So the bar is comprehension, not a complete pre-built address: given ListAgents output, an agent can determine which row corresponds to which mission, repo, and piece of work. Supplying the short hex ref is out of scope.

Verified by actually sending a message between two running missions using the new tooling, not by tests alone. Missions with no live Claude session are distinguishable from missions whose peer identity is merely unavailable. Once shipped, the /agenc-mission-messaging skill (~/app/dotfiles/claude/skills/) is updated to make the AgenC route primary and demote the direct registry read to fallback.
notes:
Surfaced in AgenC mission 591187e7-dab6-4b2d-a063-ff12220d4c3a while coordinating a YNAB backlog mission; workaround skill built in mission 7dd882f8-4ffa-4e00-987e-41432fb8134d on 2026-08-30. Skill and its design.md: ~/app/dotfiles/claude/skills/agenc-mission-messaging/

2026-08-30 — Implemented in mission f2f47c6a-638b-4892-988c-a82041d27da9. PR open, NOT merged: https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/pull/34 (branch agenc-padz-mission-peers). Ships 'agenc mission peers' (one row per addressable mission: PEER, PANE, MISSION, STATUS, REPO, TASK, with PEER and PANE verbatim as ListAgents prints them) and a 'Peer:' line on 'agenc mission inspect' that distinguishes no-live-session from running-but-unaddressable. Registry knowledge sequestered in internal/claudeconfig/session_registry.go; the server filters on PID liveness and populates transient fields, so both commands share one registry read per request.

Verified end to end: 'agenc mission peers' reported agent-dc at pane agenc-5bc1bd7b-pool:@173.%182, that row matched ListAgents verbatim, and a SendMessage addressed only from that output was delivered and answered.

Ref remains out of scope per Kevin's mid-build scope call ('we really just need a way for agents to make sense of the ListAgents output'). One ListAgents call per send is still expected.

/agenc-mission-messaging updated: AgenC commands are the primary route, registry jq lookup demoted to fallback. Two footguns found empirically and encoded there — an agenc predating the command prints 'mission' help and exits 0 rather than erroring, and a server older than the CLI silently returns no peer names.

Leave open until Kevin merges the PR and rebuilds; until then every reader of the skill takes the fallback path.

Side finding filed while verifying: agenc-6gjk (test-environment missions hit Claude Code first-run onboarding instead of the existing login; a plain 'claude' in the same directory came up authenticated).
close_reason: Merged 2026-08-30 as commit 86c5d11 via PR https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/pull/34. Ships 'agenc mission peers' and the 'Peer:' line on 'agenc mission inspect'; registry knowledge sequestered in internal/claudeconfig/session_registry.go. /agenc-mission-messaging updated to lead with the commands. Ref stays out of scope per Kevin's scope call — one ListAgents call per send is expected and accepted. Kevin still needs to rebuild his working clone and restart the agenc server for the commands to appear on his installed binary.

title: Model selection as a mission flag, plus agent-initiated model escalation
description:
GOAL (why): Kevin wants control over which Claude model an AgenC mission runs on, and — the more exciting half — for the agent itself to be able to escalate its own model when it judges the task deserves more intelligence. His capture verbatim (Todoist inbox, 2026-08-24..26): "Data point for the agency feature to allow setting models as a flag with agency missions. It would be really cool if the agent can change its own model, because then it could say something like, 'Hey, I think that this would be better done with a higher intelligence,' or something like that. That way, I could put guidance in my Claude saying that weekly planning and so on ought to be done with the highest intelligence model I have available."

The underlying interest: match model intelligence to task leverage. High-leverage IQ-sensitive work (weekly planning, foundational prompt rewrites) should be routable to the best model via standing guidance in CLAUDE.md/skills, without Kevin hand-picking per mission.

CONSTRAINTS: fit AgenC's existing mission-spawn UX (flag should feel like other `agenc mission new` flags); agent-initiated escalation must be something guidance files can reference (i.e., discoverable/invokable from inside a mission).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) a mission can be spawned with an explicit model choice via flag; (2) an agent inside a mission has a documented way to escalate/change its own model mid-work, OR the design record explains why agent-initiated escalation was rejected; (3) the capability is documented where Kevin's guidance files can point at it (so "weekly planning runs on the highest-intelligence model" is encodable).

Provenance: routed from Todoist inbox during processing, AgenC mission 3b8f684c-719a-4248-8024-b47399a1e7cb.
notes:
PARTIAL (2026-09-01, mission 1d726663-0057-4a14-af0e-80b31002daf9). PR #35 merged to main.

MET — criterion (1): a mission can be spawned with an explicit model. 'agenc mission new --model opus --effort high' works, persisted per-mission as a JSON object in the new missions.claude_args column, merged over the defaultModel/claudeArgs config chains at spawn. Allowlist lives in internal/mission/claude_args.go (ForwardedClaudeFlags); adding another forwarded Claude flag is one table entry, no migration. Closes GitHub issue #24 (ro0mquy/Yannik).

PARTIAL — criterion (3): documented so guidance files can point at it. internal/claudeconfig/adjutant_claude.md now has a 'Choosing a model or effort level per mission' section, plus docs/system-architecture.md and the generated CLI reference. Still missing: anything skill-facing, so 'weekly planning runs on the highest-intelligence model' is not yet encodable from Kevin's own CLAUDE.md/skills. That is the remaining half of this criterion.

NOT MET — criterion (2): agent-initiated mid-work model escalation. This is the more exciting half and it is untouched.

KEVIN'S DESIGN DIRECTION (verbatim, 2026-09-01): 'the way to do it, I'd imagine, would be having mission attach/reload also allow passing in those flags.' The intent: the same forwarded-flag vocabulary that 'mission new' exposes should be settable on an existing mission, so changing a running mission's model is the same gesture as choosing it at spawn rather than a separate concept. That gives an in-mission agent a real escalation path ('reload me on Opus') and gives Kevin a way to bump a mission he is watching. Treat this as the direction, not the spec — a smarter executor should work out the surface details.

What this pass already made cheap for that work: a mission's model now lives on its own DB row rather than in shared config, and the wrapper resolves it at construction, so escalation reduces to updating missions.claude_args and respawning. Open questions the escalation pass still owns: whether escalation restarts Claude immediately or only takes effect on the next spawn; whether an agent escalating itself needs a cost guardrail or an audit trail; and whether attach and reload should share one flag-parsing path with mission new (they should — ForwardedClaudeFlags is already the single source).

Storage decision and its reasoning, for whoever extends this: one keyed-JSON column, not a column per flag. Kevin's call, on the grounds that a column per flag re-introduces the per-flag tax the allowlist exists to remove — each new column needs edits in four positionally-coupled places (the shared SELECT list plus two hand-written scanners' declaration and Scan arg lists). Clone semantics: clones inherit the source mission's args, overridable, with the inheritance printed so it is never silent.

title: mission new --headless --no-focus still launched attached/focused in the tmux pool
description:
WHY: Background/fire-and-forget missions are a core AgenC pattern; if --headless grabs the user's terminal focus, every agent-spawned background mission interrupts whatever Kevin is doing, defeating the flag's purpose.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. From inside a running mission's Claude session, run: agenc mission new mieubrisse/exobrain --headless --no-focus --prompt 'anything'
2. Observe the CLI prints 'Launched in tmux pool' (the normal non-headless launch message) and the new mission opens attached/focused in the user's terminal.

OBSERVED (2026-08-19 10:32 EDT): From inside mission fe0f46c5-1f02-418d-8707-768ba47de957, the above spawn produced mission ce43cff3-efdd-4483-b1b0-4959d54c4c87, which started in the FOREGROUND (attached), stealing focus — Kevin observed this directly.

EXPECTED: --headless help text says 'run in headless mode (no terminal, outputs to log)', and --no-focus says don't focus the new mission's tmux window. Neither behavior held.

NOTES: The mission itself ran fine (wrapper.log streaming events normally), so the defect is launch/focus behavior only. Unknown whether --headless is ignored entirely when spawned from within another mission's Claude session, or whether the tmux pool is the intended headless vehicle and only the focus/attach is the bug — worth checking both flags' handling.
acceptance_criteria: Repro (agenc mission new <repo> --headless --no-focus --prompt '...' from inside a mission's Claude session) launches the mission with no terminal attach and no tmux focus change; CLI output reflects the headless path. Root cause identified for why the 2026-08-19 spawn attached.
notes: Executing AgenC mission: 3bd7f556-2339-42f4-8d00-44afdf68ef0d (foreground, spawned 2026-08-19 from inbox-processing mission fe0f46c5-1f02-418d-8707-768ba47de957 at Kevin's request).
close_reason: Root cause: the CLI dropped --headless on the wire. Commit e5006ad (2026-02-28) removed Headless from the CreateMissionRequest the CLI sends, encoding headless intent as 'empty TmuxSession' — equivalent at the time. Commit eeace1a (2026-05-26) added server-side parent link-set mirroring for source=mission spawns, guarded by req.Headless — but no CLI path had set that field since February, so --headless from inside a mission was silently ignored: the server mirrored the parent's tmux link-set and linked the child window into Kevin's session (= attached). --no-focus WAS honored (no select-window occurred; link-window uses -d) — the 'foreground' observation was the window being linked into the active session. Cron headless kept working by accident (source=cron falls into the TmuxSession-based branch). The CLI message bug compounded it: 'Launched in tmux pool' printed whenever source=mission, even headless. FIX (commit b2593ee): wire Headless:headlessFlag into all three CreateMissionRequest literals in cmd/mission_new.go; extract printLaunchDestination() which checks headless first and prints 'Running headless (pool window; not linked to any tmux session)'; 2 new E2E tests. Server needed no change — running server already honors req.Headless, so the fixed CLI alone fixes behavior. VERIFIED: make build + make e2e (144 pass/0 fail); live repro of the bead's exact command from inside mission 3bd7f556 (parent linked in hyperspace2): new mission 4e2fb5d0 landed ONLY in agenc-pool, active windows in deepwork/hyperspace2 unchanged, CLI reported headless path; repro mission removed after. Follow-up: dead Wrapper.RunHeadless + arch-doc drift filed as a separate bead.

title: AgenC-generated permission rules use non-canonical tool verbs -> dozens of 'not matched by file permission checks' startup warnings per mission (GH #21)
description:
WHY: Every mission startup prints dozens of Claude Code warnings (Kevin counted 154) of the form: "Permission allow/deny/ask rule (<file>): <Verb>(<path>) is not matched by file permission checks — only Read(path)/Edit(path) rules are. Use Read/Edit(<path>) instead." ROOT CAUSE: Claude Code's FILE-permission matcher only recognizes Read(path) [covers ALL file-reading tools: Read, Glob, Grep] and Edit(path) [covers ALL file-editing tools: Edit, Write, NotebookEdit]. AgenC's generated permission entries use the tool-SPECIFIC verbs — Glob(...), Grep(...), Write(...), NotebookEdit(...) — which Claude Code ignores for file-permission checks, so each one emits a warning. Result: a noisy wall on every mission startup, and it signals AgenC emits non-canonical permission entries.

TWO SOURCES contribute (full warning dump in NOTES):
1. agenc-settings.json — AgenC's GENERATED per-mission op-settings. THIS IS THE PRIMARY, IN-SCOPE FIX (AgenC code). The op-settings permission builders emit these — grep internal/claudeconfig/overrides.go + merge.go + operational_settings.go for where Glob(/Grep(/Write(/NotebookEdit( permission strings are constructed (BuildAgentDirAllowEntries, BuildRepoLibraryDenyEntries, mergeAgencSandbox, and any sibling). They must emit Read(path) for file-READ access and Edit(path) for file-EDIT/WRITE access instead. Leave non-file permissions (Bash/Skill/WebFetch/mcp__/etc.) unchanged.
2. ~/.claude/settings.json — the USER's own global config independently uses the same non-canonical verbs. The AgenC code fix will NOT touch the user's config -> OUT OF SCOPE for this bead's code change (the user fixes their own settings, or a separate 'agenc doctor' check flags it — worth noting, not fixing here).

FIX (intent — a smarter executor improves the how): collapse AgenC's file-path permission entries to the canonical Read(path)/Edit(path) forms Claude Code recognizes (Read subsumes Glob+Grep; Edit subsumes Write+NotebookEdit), verified against Claude Code's documented permission semantics. Follow repo conventions: invoke /brainstorm before implementing; make check + make e2e must be green; ideally add an assertion (unit on the op-settings builder, or e2e) that generated file-path permissions use ONLY Read/Edit.
acceptance_criteria: A freshly spawned mission produces ZERO 'not matched by file permission checks' warnings that originate from agenc-settings.json (the AgenC-generated op-settings). The user's own ~/.claude/settings.json warnings are out of scope for this bead. make check + make e2e green.
notes:
GH issue #21. Surfaced during the State-Y flip wrap-up (mission 363f43aa-b09e-41b0-bf41-89b1479dc26a); Kevin wants this addressed in a FORKED mission. Full warning dump Kevin observed (2026-08-03) — note the two source files: "../../../../.claude/settings.json" = user's global; "../agenc-settings.json" = AgenC's generated op-settings (the in-scope target):

--- agenc-settings.json (AGENC — FIX THESE) examples ---
Glob(./**) -> use Read(./**)
Glob(./*) -> use Read(./*)
Glob(//Users/odyssey/.agenc/missions/<uuid>/agent/**) -> Read(...)
Glob(~/.agenc/missions/<uuid>/agent/**) -> Read(...)
Write(./**) -> Edit(./**)
Write(~/.agenc/missions/<uuid>/agent/**) -> Edit(...)
NotebookEdit(./**) -> Edit(./**)
NotebookEdit(~/.agenc/missions/<uuid>/agent/*) -> Edit(...)
Write(//Users/odyssey/.agenc/repos/**) [deny] -> Edit(...)
NotebookEdit(~/.agenc/repos/**) [deny] -> Edit(...)

--- ~/.claude/settings.json (USER — out of scope, note only) examples ---
Glob(${HOME}/app/exobrain/**) -> Read(...) ; Glob(~/.beads/shared-server/**) ; Write(${HOME}/app/exobrain/**) -> Edit ; Write(~/.agenc/server/server.sock) -> Edit ; Write(*.env)[deny] -> Edit ; Glob(*.env)[deny] -> Read ; Write(claude/settings.json)[ask] -> Edit

Pattern is uniform: every Glob(P)/Grep(P) file-read rule should be Read(P); every Write(P)/NotebookEdit(P) file-edit rule should be Edit(P). The agenc-settings.json half is the AgenC generator bug to fix.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 7d779b4: op-settings + adjutant permission builders now emit only canonical Read(path)/Edit(path) verbs. Verified: unit guard test asserts only Read/Edit, concrete generated agenc-settings.json shows zero non-canonical file-path rules, make check + make e2e green. Follow-up (out of scope): user's own ~/.claude/settings.json uses the same bad pattern.

title: Bound ~/.claude.json trust-entry accumulation at scale (State Y)
description: WHY: State Y consolidates EVERY non-archived mission's trust entry into the single shared ~/.claude.json (State X isolated each in its own per-mission snapshot). Verified working in production — prune is exact (2660 entries == 2660 non-archived missions, 0 dead) and no corruption — but it surfaces a scaling property: at 2660 non-archived missions the file is already ~531KB and grows with all-time non-archived mission count. Every trust write AND every Claude-side write is a read-modify-write of the WHOLE file, so (a) the concurrent-clobber risk scales with file size, and (b) the prune only bounds the file by ARCHIVAL — archived/deleted missions are pruned, but non-archived accumulate. For a heavy user who rarely archives, the file grows unboundedly (and Claude Code parses the whole thing on startup). Needs a decision on how to bound it.
design: Options Kevin floated (2026-08-03), no decision yet: (a) a job/cron that removes trust entries for long-ago / dormant missions — an AGE-based prune beyond just 'archived'; (b) leave them and accept growth (cheapest, but the concurrent-write risk + Claude parse cost grow with the file); (c) an explicit 'agenc' command to prune trust entries; (d) seed trust LAZILY at respawn rather than eagerly for all non-archived missions — most dormant missions never respawn, so they never need a trust entry in the first place, which attacks the root. Executor's call; must not break respawn-trust for a dormant mission that DOES come back (option d needs a create/respawn-time seed).
acceptance_criteria: ~/.claude.json's mission-trust footprint stays bounded — it does not grow without limit as the all-time non-archived mission count climbs — while a mission that respawns still gets trusted without a dialog.
notes: Surfaced 2026-08-03 inspecting the REAL ~/.claude.json during Kevin's State-Y go-live test (mission 07f685ed): 2660 non-archived missions -> 531KB file, up from ~200KB backups. State-Y flip = mission 363f43aa / GitHub issue #13 / bead agenc-lh8p. Folds together with agenc-c4ko (the cleanup-loop->trust-prune bead the flip already implemented for the archived/deleted case) — this bead is the AGE/SCALE dimension c4ko didn't cover.

title: Make e2e repo-add tests deterministic (remove live-GitHub dependency)
description: WHY: the e2e suite's 'agenc repo add' tests clone from github.com, so they FAIL when the environment can't reach GitHub — an environmental failure indistinguishable (to a naive reader or an autonomous agent) from a real code regression. This makes a green 'make e2e' network-dependent and AMBIGUOUS. Dangerous for autonomy: an agent seeing 140/143 offline may misreport a regression, or worse, learn to ignore e2e failures entirely. Make the repo-add tests deterministic so 'green' means the same thing regardless of network weather.
design: Prefer a LOCAL FIXTURE repo: have 'make test-env' create a small throwaway git repo on local disk, and point the repo-add tests at a file:// path instead of a github URL (same code path, zero network). Fallback if a real remote is genuinely needed: gate on network-availability and print a VISIBLE NAMED SKIP when offline (never silently count environmental as pass or fail). ~3 tests affected today (e.g. 'repo add for mv test', 'repo add with --description succeeds').
acceptance_criteria: 'make e2e' produces the same pass/fail result online and offline; no test fails (or silently passes) due solely to GitHub reachability.
notes: Surfaced during the State-Y flip (mission 363f43aa-b09e-41b0-bf41-89b1479dc26a) auditing whether e2e is a trustworthy autonomy enabler. Sibling to agenc-se8o (the merge-gate bead) — a required gate is only trustworthy if green is unambiguous.

title: Add an e2e harness canary (self-check that the suite can still detect failures)
description: WHY: the e2e suite could silently degrade so assertions can no longer fail — this is not hypothetical: the State-Y flip found a MANDATORY '--settings union' assertion that grepped a file the test itself wrote, so it literally could not fail, yet showed green. If that drift spread, 'make e2e' could report a proud 143/143 while testing nothing — and be trusted. Add a canary: a harness self-test that proves failure-detection still works, so a neutered suite surfaces as a LOUD abort instead of a false green.
design: At the start of scripts/e2e-test.sh, run a deliberately-FALSE assertion in a controlled way and confirm the harness registers it as a failure — e.g. assert 'false' exits 0 (it exits 1, so this MUST be detected as a failure); if the harness instead reports pass, abort with a FATAL 'e2e harness no longer detects failures' and a non-zero exit, BEFORE running the real suite. Keep the canary isolated so it never pollutes the real pass/fail counts. This is the 'check-loop for the check-loop' (Pair Every Loop With a Check-Loop).
acceptance_criteria: If the run_test / output-assertion failure-detection is broken (any known-false assertion stops failing), 'make e2e' aborts loudly with a clear harness-broken message rather than reporting green.
notes: Surfaced during the State-Y flip (mission 363f43aa-b09e-41b0-bf41-89b1479dc26a); directly motivated by the theater assertion caught + fixed in that flip. Sibling to agenc-se8o (merge gate) and the repo-add-determinism bead — together they make a green e2e trustworthy enough to gate merges on.

title: Enforce make e2e as an automatic merge gate (PR flow / required CI check)
description: WHY: AgenC's e2e suite (scripts/e2e-test.sh, 'make e2e') is the primary BEHAVIORAL safety net that makes autonomous agent work trustworthy — but it runs MANUAL-ONLY today. The pre-commit hook runs 'make check' (compile + unit tests), which does NOT include e2e; no CI runs e2e. So a behavioral regression surfaces only when a human or agent remembers to run 'make e2e' before merging. That is a silent-rot risk (the 'Pair Every Loop With a Check-Loop' failure mode): the check exists but nothing forces it to run, so its value degrades precisely on unattended/autonomous changes. Establish a flow that makes a green 'make e2e' a REQUIRED gate before changes land on main, running automatically on every change rather than on memory. Kevin is not ready to stand up the full PR flow yet (2026-08-03) — this captures the intent for when he is.
design: Mechanism is open (executor's call, fit AgenC's solo-repo workflow — no heavyweight process Kevin doesn't want): a GitHub PR flow with branch protection + a required status check that runs 'make e2e'; OR a CI workflow; OR an AgenC cron that blocks/flags. The intent is 'e2e cannot be silently skipped before merge', not a specific tool. Note the current pre-commit hook only runs 'make check' — extending it to e2e locally is a partial option but doesn't cover the 'agent forgets / bypasses' case the way a required remote check does.
acceptance_criteria: A change that breaks an e2e test cannot reach main without the failure being surfaced automatically — no reliance on a human or agent remembering to run 'make e2e'.
notes: Surfaced during the State-Y flip (mission 363f43aa-b09e-41b0-bf41-89b1479dc26a) when Kevin asked whether the e2e is a trustworthy autonomy enabler. Audit found the suite structurally healthy (~95% genuine assertions, theater-free after fixing one --settings assertion, reproducible 143/143) but MANUAL-ONLY. Sibling e2e-hardening concerns (GitHub-clone network non-determinism + a harness self-check canary) may warrant their own bead — a required gate is only as trustworthy as the suite's determinism + honesty.

title: Close JSONC devcontainer.json issues #17 + #8 as wontfix after devcontainer removal
description:
GitHub issues #17 (swade1987) and #8 (omar-augur) report the SAME root cause: AgenC parses a repo's devcontainer.json with strict encoding/json, which chokes on JSONC comments (// and /* */) and aborts wrapper init at internal/wrapper/wrapper.go:247 (generating devcontainer overlay). devcontainer.json is JSONC by spec, so comments are common and this makes affected repos impossible to open.

WHY wontfix rather than fix-the-parser: Kevin decided to remove AgenC's devcontainer-reading infrastructure entirely (bead agenc-ok7h, part of the State Y work). Once the overlay generator and the whole devcontainer read path are gone, there is NO code path that parses devcontainer.json — the JSONC bug ceases to exist because the feature does. So the correct resolution for #17 and #8 is wontfix-by-removal, not a JSONC-aware parser.

Both issues are USER-FILED bug reports (swade1987 = Steve Wade; omar-augur hit it on a fresh install). They deserve a clear, kind close explaining that AgenC removed devcontainer support by design rather than fixing the parser, and what that means for them.

Issues: https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/issues/17 and https://github.com/mieubrisse/agenc/issues/8
acceptance_criteria: 1. Devcontainer removal (agenc-ok7h) has actually shipped/merged before either issue is closed. 2. Both #17 and #8 closed as not-planned/wontfix, each with a clear explanation that devcontainer support was removed by design (link the removal PR/commit), written respectfully to a user. 3. The close posts use the /github-posting AgenC-authored disclosure prefix and /user-support-voice; framed via /addressing-user-github-issue. 4. #8's existing comment is read and addressed if it adds context.
notes: Filed 2026-07-28 during the agenc-ok7h brainstorm (mission cc8e4c39-e2ca-45d5-8818-907de7cfbece) at Kevin's request. Deferred: do NOT close until the removal merges. Both issues share one root cause (strict JSON parse of devcontainer.json); close together.
close_reason: Closed GH #17 (swade1987) and #8 (omar-augur) as not-planned, each with a close-the-loop comment in Kevin's support voice (proofreader-gated, AgenC disclosure prefix): owned the strict-JSON-parse-of-JSONC root cause, explained the resolution (devcontainer support removed entirely in agenc-ok7h, so the crash is gone and missions run host-only), surfaced the host-only tradeoff, invited feedback without over-committing Kevin. Both now CLOSED/NOT_PLANNED.

title: agenc session print fails on long jsonl lines: bufio.Scanner token too long

It currently fails with 'error reading session file: bufio.Scanner: token too long' (session_print.go:119 -> session.FormatConversation) on transcripts containing a very long single jsonl line (e.g., large embedded tool results/images). The transcript is healthy on disk; only the reader chokes — which silently masquerades as data loss. title: Deploy the AgenC fleet to Kevin's Ubuntu VPS — 24/7 capacity per gated work class (autonomy program S3)
description:
**Why:** When Kevin's laptop closes, the fleet stops — his Max subscription sits idle. He owns an idle Ubuntu VPS. 2. title: Notification picker: pressing Enter on mission-less notification doesn't mark it read
description:
When a user presses Enter on an `agenc notification` entry that has no mission attached, the picker opens but the notification is not marked as read. title: agenc server: FD exhaustion (EMFILE) — leak hunt; search indexer is prime suspect
description:
The agenc server hit file descriptor exhaustion (EMFILE / 'too many open files') on 2026-06-07 ~19:52 local and stayed degraded for ~19 min until killed by SIGTERM at 20:11:07, then restarted cleanly.

During the window every fd-touching subsystem failed in cascade:
- Unix socket accept on server.sock (all CLI/UI calls rejected — server was unreachable from the user's perspective)
- Config reads (~/.agenc/config/config.yml)
- Tmux keybindings writes (~/.agenc/tmux-keybindings.conf)
- git subprocess invocations (couldn't 'open /dev/null')
- Search indexer file extraction
- Config-watcher shadow-repo ingest of CLAUDE.md

HOT LEAD: the search indexer logged the same file failing on every ~30s tick during the entire window:
  open /Users/odyssey/.claude/projects/-Users-odyssey--agenc-missions-35542fec-5b20-474b-b391-a4e85df8d608-agent/6f1ea3c3-462f-4bf0-b296-325bc462a079.jsonl: too many open files

That repetition on a single file is suggestive of an fd leak in the search indexer's content-extraction path — likely an os.Open / OpenFile without guaranteed Close() on some error branch, applied repeatedly to the same target. Worth auditing first before casting a wider net. The indexer might also just be the loudest victim of a leak that lives elsewhere (writeable-copy git invocations, request handlers, fsnotify watchers, etc.); rule it out either way.

Logs:
- ~/.agenc/server/server.log
- First 'too many open files': 2026/06/07 19:52:01
- Restart line: 2026/06/07 20:11:09 'Server listening on /Users/odyssey/.agenc/server/server.sock'

Secondary observation worth its own bead later: when a git subprocess fails with EMFILE, the writeable-copy reconciler at internal/server/writeable_copies.go (runWriteableCopyTick) classifies the repo as 'git_corrupt' and auto-PAUSEs it. Two writeable-copies (alembiq, dotfiles) were falsely paused during this incident — both auto-resumed on server restart, but the pause heuristic should distinguish 'git failed because EMFILE' from real corruption.

title: AgenC: tighten parent-child mission relationship; add wait + explicit-ownership controls
description:
Surfaced during the REFLECT phase of a /diamond-cascade session redesigning /weekly-plan → /build-weekly-plan (AgenC mission 06d4403f-2ada-4289-a321-09f8b2a1c99e, 2026-06-07). /five-whys analysis traced one of the session's load-bearing failures (Failure D — 'verify each fix landed almost slipped') to a missing parent-child mission ownership model.

THE PATTERN — Kevin's framing:

Parent missions spawn side missions via 'agenc mission new', then implicitly treat them as 'spawned and forgotten' — 'OK, it spawned you, can monitor it' — without active follow-up or verification. Side missions write to separate repos and notify on completion via tmux notifications, but parent missions don't reliably READ the produced artifact before declaring their own work done. In the originating session, the parent mission almost moved on from EXECUTE without verifying that the side mission's template edit landed (the side mission HAD deviated badly from spec; the parent mission would have missed it). Kevin had to manually check by asking 'did you ensure the side mission landed?'.

KEVIN'S FRAMING:

Parent missions should be CLEARLY responsible for child missions. The user explicitly takes over ownership at a defined handoff. Until then, the parent owns it. Today's tooling doesn't make this ownership relationship structural — it's left to convention + agent attention.

CONCRETE CAPABILITY NEEDS (Kevin's, off the top):

1. **Wait on sub-missions** — 'agenc mission wait <id>' or equivalent, so parent can synchronously block on child completion rather than fire-and-forget. The Bash tool's run_in_background + subagent task-notification model works for subagents in the same process; sub-missions need an analogous wait primitive.
2. **Cleaner ownership semantics** — explicit 'parent owns this child until handoff' framing in the spawn/inspect tooling. Possibly: 'mission inspect' shows parent + ownership state.
3. **Verification-by-default** — parent expected to read child's produced artifact before declaring own work done. May land as tooling or as a CLAUDE.md/skill rule enforced via the parent's workflow.

FOLDS IN:

- L6/F4 from the originating session's REFLECT phase — 'verify each fix landed' rule should extend to delegated work. The deeper fix is at the AgenC infrastructure level (give parent missions the tools to wait + own + verify) rather than the CLAUDE.md doc level. Documenting this as a CLAUDE.md rule alone would be the WRONG level — agents would still forget without the structural support.

Provenance: derived from /five-whys analysis (Failure D) in the originating session. Full session transcript: agenc mission print 06d4403f-2ada-4289-a321-09f8b2a1c99e.
notes:
DATA POINTS — additional cases observed

### 2026-06-07 — AgenC mission 778812a8 (cc-rules skill creation cascade)

Parent /diamond-cascade mission spawned child mission 35542fec to land artifacts in the Alembiq repo (different repo than parent). Work was transferred via beads issue alembiq-cggt with verbatim file artifacts in the notes field.

Parent's wait mechanism was a Bash `run_in_background` with an until-loop polling `agenc mission inspect | grep "Status:.*IDLE"`. This is a workaround for the missing wait primitive (need #1 in the original framing).

Failure modes observed:

1. **Parent went effectively idle while waiting.** The user had to type "should be done now" to nudge the parent into checking. Without the nudge, the parent had no engagement model with the in-flight wait — the background poll would have eventually fired, but the parent was not actively reflecting on it. When the poll did eventually fire (after the user nudge + manual verification was already complete), the notification arrived as redundant noise. Reinforces need #1 (proper wait primitive) and need #2 (ownership semantics — the parent was not behaviorally owning the child).

2. **Verification by default was carried out — but only because of an unrelated CLAUDE.md rule.** Parent did read the actual landed files rather than trusting child's "PASS" close summary, because the CLAUDE.md "Apply the same skepticism to your own prior outputs" rule extends to delegated work in practice. But this verification was carried out under that rule, not as a structural property of the parent-child relationship. Without that rule, parent would have defaulted to trusting the child's summary. Reinforces need #3 (verification-by-default).

3. **Bead-as-transfer-medium worked well** — but is orthogonal to the ownership problem. The bead structure made the artifacts persistent and reviewable, and the child's bd close note documented its work. Worth noting as a positive: a structured transfer artifact (bead) is complementary to, not a substitute for, parent-side ownership.

Provenance: AgenC mission 778812a8-9bd0-406b-a6a3-f75441329b61, session e1214942. Child mission 35542fec-5b20-474b-b391-a4e85df8d608. Transfer bead alembiq-cggt (in mieubrisse/alembiq .beads). Replay: `agenc session print e1214942 --all`.
